title: Booting, GRUB, systemd & shutdown
about: What happens between power-on and the login prompt: firmware, partition tables, boot loader, kernel, the first process, systemd units and targets, managing services with systemctl, and shutting down cleanly.

questions.title: The boot sequence
questions.text: Put the stages of booting a typical Linux PC in order.

items.t: The firmware (BIOS or UEFI) tests and initialises the hardware
items.why: Nothing can be loaded before the hardware is usable.

items.t: The firmware finds the boot disk and reads its partition table and boot code
items.why: It must know where the boot loader lives.

items.t: The boot loader (for example GRUB) runs and lets you choose a kernel or system
items.why: Stage 1 loads stage 2, which shows the menu.

items.t: The kernel is loaded into memory and starts (with an initial RAM disk)
items.why: The loader hands control over to it.

items.t: The kernel starts the first process (PID 1, normally systemd)
Services start and a login prompt appears
items.why: The system is ready for users.

questions.title: What firmware does
questions.text: What is the job of the firmware (BIOS or UEFI) at power-on?

options.t: To initialise and check the basic hardware and then locate and start a boot loader from a storage device.
options.why: It lives in non-volatile memory on the motherboard.

options.t: To load the kernel modules of the operating system.
To start the user's login shell.

questions.title: Why a boot loader
questions.text: Why is a boot loader such as GRUB needed between the firmware and the kernel?

options.t: The firmware can load only a small piece of code, while the loader understands file systems, can offer a menu, and can load a large kernel and its initial RAM disk with options.
The kernel cannot run without a graphical menu.
The firmware cannot read any disk.
options.why: It can read the first blocks or the EFI partition.

options.t: GRUB replaces the kernel after boot.

questions.title: BIOS and UEFI ideas
questions.text: Match each term with its description.

pairs.r: The older firmware that boots from the first sector (MBR) of a disk
The modern firmware interface, able to start boot loaders from a special FAT partition
A UEFI feature that only starts boot software signed with trusted keys
The old partition table and boot sector layout
The newer partition table that supports many partitions and very large disks

extras.why: None of the terms above is that; GRUB, for one, is a boot loader.

questions.title: MBR limits
questions.text: Which limitation belongs to the classic MBR partitioning scheme?

options.t: At most four primary partitions (or three plus an extended one holding logical partitions), and disks beyond about 2 TB cannot be addressed.
It cannot hold a Linux file system.
It is limited to a single partition.

questions.title: GPT advantages
questions.text: Which is an advantage of GPT over MBR?

options.t: It supports many more partitions (128 by default) and much larger disks, stores a backup copy of the table, and identifies partitions with unique IDs (GUIDs).
It is required for any disk smaller than 1 GB.

options.why: It is used for 64-bit systems as well.

questions.title: The EFI system partition
questions.text: Where does a UEFI system normally keep its boot loaders?

options.t: On a small FAT-formatted partition called the EFI System Partition (ESP), often mounted at `/boot/efi`.
In the first 446 bytes of the disk only.
options.why: That is the BIOS/MBR boot code area.
Configuration fragments, not the boot loader.

questions.title: Legacy mode
questions.text: What does "legacy mode" (CSM) mean on a UEFI machine?

options.t: The firmware behaves like a BIOS and boots from the MBR, so old systems can still start.
options.why: The installation mode must match the partitioning scheme.

questions.title: GRUB files
questions.text: Match each file or directory with its role.

pairs.r: The configuration that GRUB reads at boot
pairs.why: Normally generated, not edited by hand.

pairs.r: General settings such as the default entry and time-out
Scripts that produce parts of the menu
The command that rebuilds `grub.cfg`
Writes GRUB to a disk

extras.why: That is `grub.cfg`; `/etc/fstab` lists file systems to mount.

questions.title: Editing grub.cfg
questions.text: On Ubuntu and Debian, why should you not edit `/boot/grub/grub.cfg` directly?

options.t: It is generated by `update-grub` from `/etc/default/grub` and `/etc/grub.d/`, so manual changes are overwritten.
Because it is a binary file.
Because only the kernel can write to `/boot`.

questions.title: Regenerate the menu
questions.text: After changing `/etc/default/grub`, rebuild the boot menu with: `{{0}}`

wrong.why: That writes the boot loader to a disk; it does not regenerate the menu.
That builds the initial RAM disk.

questions.title: What GRUB can do
questions.text: Which of these can GRUB do?

options.t: Show a menu of systems and kernels, edit boot options, offer a command line, and chain-load other boot loaders such as Windows'.

options.why: That is the job of PID 1.

options.t: Replace the file system driver of the kernel.

questions.title: Rescue with GRUB
questions.text: The system does not boot because of a broken menu entry. What does GRUB's command line let you do?

options.t: Set the root device, load a kernel and an initial RAM disk by hand, and boot, to get the machine started and repair it.
Edit the passwords of users directly.
Nothing, GRUB has no interactive mode.

questions.title: Manual boot from the GRUB prompt
questions.text: Put the GRUB commands in order to start a Linux system by hand.

items.why: Choose the partition that holds the kernel.
Load the kernel and tell it where the root file system is.

questions.title: What the kernel does first
questions.text: After the boot loader hands over control, what does the kernel do before it starts the first process?

options.t: It detects the CPU and memory, sets up memory management and interrupts, initialises devices and drivers, mounts the root file system and then starts PID 1.
It starts all the daemons itself.
It asks the user which services to start.

questions.title: initrd
questions.text: What is the initial RAM disk (initrd / initramfs)?

options.t: A small temporary root file system loaded into memory with the kernel, holding the drivers and tools needed to find and mount the real root file system.
options.why: Discarded after the real root is mounted.

options.t: A backup of the user's home directory.
A list of services to start.

questions.title: Root mounted read-only
questions.text: Why does the kernel often mount the root file system read-only at first?

options.t: So that it can be checked (fsck) safely before anything writes to it; it is remounted read-write later in the boot.
Because it cannot write until the first login.
Because the root disk is always a CD.
Because permissions forbid root to write.

questions.title: Low PIDs
questions.text: Match each process with its role.

pairs.r: The kernel's idle/scheduler task (not a normal process)
The first user-space process, `init`, today usually `systemd`
The parent of kernel threads
Presents the login prompt

extras.r: The first process of the machine, `bash`
extras.why: Your shell comes much later, started by PID 1 through login.

questions.title: Kernel messages
questions.text: Which command shows the messages the kernel printed during boot (hardware detection, drivers)?

options.why: It prints the kernel ring buffer.
Shows the kernel name and version only.

questions.title: Kernel parameters
questions.text: What can you pass to the kernel from the boot loader?

options.t: Options such as the root device, `single` or `systemd.unit=rescue.target` to boot into a repair mode, or `init=/bin/bash`.
options.why: They modify how the kernel and PID 1 start.

options.t: The date for the next shutdown.

questions.title: The first process
questions.text: What is the role of the process with PID 1?

options.t: It starts and supervises the system's services, adopts orphaned processes and gives access to the system (logins).
options.why: On modern Linux it is usually systemd.

options.t: It is the same as the kernel.
It is the first user's shell.
options.why: It starts before any user logs in.

questions.title: Kinds of init system
questions.text: Match each system with its family.

pairs.r: The classic sequential start with scripts in `/etc/init.d`
The modern parallel, dependency-based manager, standard on most distributions
The init system of macOS
The approach of FreeBSD, OpenBSD and NetBSD

extras.r: The init system of Linux, GRUB
extras.why: GRUB is the boot loader; it runs before the init system.

questions.title: Advantages of systemd
questions.text: Select the features that systemd offers.

options.t: Starts services in parallel, following declared dependencies.
Tracks the processes of a service with control groups (cgroups), not just PIDs.
options.why: Finds all children of a service.

options.t: Can start services on demand (for example when a socket or device appears).
Needs a graphical desktop to work.

options.why: It runs on top of it.

questions.title: What is a unit
questions.text: What is a systemd "unit"?

options.t: A configuration file describing something systemd manages: a service, a mount, a socket, a timer, a target...
options.why: Named with a suffix such as `.service` or `.target`.
A unit describes it; the process is separate.

questions.title: Unit types
questions.text: Match each unit type with its purpose.

pairs.r: A daemon or program that systemd runs
A group of units that marks a state of the system
A file system mount point
pairs.why: Generated from `/etc/fstab` or written by hand.

pairs.r: A schedule that triggers another unit
A network or local socket that can start a service on demand

extras.why: Accounts live in `/etc/passwd`; `.user` is not a unit type.

questions.title: Where units live
questions.text: Where are the unit files shipped by packages usually stored, and where do administrators put their own changes?

options.t: Packages install them under `/lib/systemd/system` (or `/usr/lib/systemd/system`); local units and overrides go in `/etc/systemd/system`, which takes precedence.
options.why: Do not edit the package files.

options.t: In the user's home directory only.

questions.title: What a target is
questions.text: What is a target in systemd?

options.t: A named group of units that represents a stage or state of the system, replacing the older runlevels.
options.why: Reaching a target means its units are started.

options.t: A file that stores the partition table.
A way to direct output to the printer.

questions.title: Runlevels and targets
questions.text: Match each classic runlevel with its systemd target.

pairs.r: `poweroff.target`
`rescue.target`
`multi-user.target`
`graphical.target`
`reboot.target`

extras.why: That is a real target, but it has no classic runlevel number.

questions.title: Default target
questions.text: Which command shows the target that the system boots into?

options.why: Often `graphical.target` on desktops and `multi-user.target` on servers.
Shows the state of the system and services.
Only reports the runlevel on some systems.

questions.title: Change target now
questions.text: What does `systemctl isolate rescue.target` do?

options.t: It stops all the services that do not belong to the rescue target and brings the machine into single-user maintenance mode.
options.why: It switches the running system to that target.

options.t: It makes rescue mode the default for all future boots.

questions.title: Set the default
questions.text: Make the system boot to text mode (without graphical login) next time: `systemctl {{0}} multi-user.target`
questions.note: `isolate` switches now; `set-default` decides the next boots.

wrong.why: That changes the running state now but not the next boot.
That enables a unit to start at boot; it does not choose the default target.

questions.title: Basic systemctl actions
questions.text: Match each command with its effect.

pairs.r: Start the service now
pairs.why: It runs until stopped or shutdown.

pairs.r: Stop the service now
pairs.why: It stays enabled for the next boot if it was.

pairs.r: Stop and start it again
Show its state, recent log lines and whether it is enabled
Ask it to re-read its configuration without stopping
pairs.why: Only if the service supports it.

extras.why: None of these commands does that; `systemctl cups` without an action is not even valid.

questions.title: enable versus start
questions.text: What is the difference between `systemctl start ssh` and `systemctl enable ssh`?

options.t: `start` runs the service now; `enable` makes it start automatically at boot but does not start it now.
`start` makes it start at every boot.
options.why: It affects the current session only.

questions.title: disable versus stop
questions.text: What does `systemctl disable ssh` do?

options.t: It removes the automatic start at boot but leaves the running service running.
options.why: Combine with `stop` to end it now.

options.t: It prevents the service from ever being started, even manually.

questions.title: Mask
questions.text: What does `systemctl mask ssh` achieve beyond `disable`?

options.t: It links the unit to `/dev/null`, so it cannot be started at all, neither at boot nor manually nor as a dependency.

questions.title: Start and enable together
questions.text: Start the service now and also at every boot: `systemctl {{0}} ssh`
questions.note: Equivalent to `systemctl enable ssh` followed by `systemctl start ssh`.

wrong.why: It would run the service but not enable it for boot.

questions.title: Is it running
questions.text: Which command prints `active` or `inactive` for a service so a script can test it?

options.why: Its exit status is 0 when the unit is active.

questions.title: Old-style commands
questions.text: On many systems `service cups start` and `/etc/init.d/cups start` still exist. What are they?

options.t: The System V ways of controlling a service; with systemd the `service` command simply forwards to `systemctl`, while calling the script in `/etc/init.d` directly bypasses systemd's tracking and is discouraged.
The only possible ways on any system.

options.why: Regular users may need `sudo` for both.

questions.title: Service logs
questions.text: Which command shows the log messages of the service `ssh` collected by systemd?

options.why: Reads the journal and filters by unit.

questions.title: Failed units
questions.text: Which command lists the units that failed to start?

options.why: A quick health check after boot.
Follows new messages, not failed units.
Reports the enabled state of one unit.

questions.title: Dependencies
questions.text: What does it mean when a unit file says `After=network.target` and `Wants=network.target`?

options.t: The service is started after the network target is reached, and systemd tries to bring the network up as well.
options.why: `After` sets ordering; `Wants` sets a soft dependency.

options.t: The service starts before the network target.
The service is deleted when the network goes down.

questions.title: Restart on failure
questions.text: Which setting in a service unit makes systemd start the program again when it crashes?

questions.title: Shutdown commands
questions.text: Match each command with its effect.

pairs.r: Halt and power off immediately
Reboot in five minutes
Power off at 15:20
Cancel a scheduled shutdown
Restart the machine

extras.r: Kill every user session and delete their files
extras.why: No option does that; `shutdown -k` only sends the warnings, without shutting down.

questions.title: Who can shut down
questions.text: Who may normally run `shutdown` on a multi-user system?

options.t: Only the first user who logged in.

questions.title: What happens at shutdown
questions.text: Put the stages of a clean shutdown in order.

items.t: Users are warned with a message
items.why: So they can save their work.

items.t: Processes receive `SIGTERM` and services are stopped in order
Processes that survive the grace period receive `SIGKILL`
File systems are synchronised and unmounted
items.why: Write buffers to disk, then detach.

items.t: The machine powers off or reboots

questions.title: Why SIGTERM first
questions.text: Why does the shutdown sequence send `SIGTERM` before `SIGKILL`?

options.t: Programs can catch `SIGTERM` to save data and exit cleanly; only those that do not finish in time are killed with `SIGKILL`.

questions.title: Why unmount
questions.text: Why must file systems be unmounted (or remounted read-only) before power off?

options.t: Data may still be waiting in memory buffers; unmounting writes it to disk and marks the file system clean, preventing corruption.
options.why: A sudden power cut can leave inconsistencies.

options.t: Because unmounted disks use less electricity.
Because the kernel would otherwise refuse to power off.

questions.title: Custom shutdown message
questions.text: Which command warns users with your own message and shuts down in 10 minutes?

options.why: The text is sent to all terminals.
The message is not read from stdin.

questions.title: Reboot shortcut
questions.text: What is a normal effect of pressing `Ctrl+Alt+Del` on a Linux text console?

options.t: It triggers a reboot through the init system (systemd maps it to `reboot.target`).
options.why: On many systems it can be disabled.
The kernel passes the key combination to the init system.

questions.title: fstab
questions.text: What is `/etc/fstab` used for?

options.t: It lists the file systems (device, mount point, type, options) that are mounted at boot.

questions.title: Swap
questions.text: What is swap space?

options.t: Disk space that the kernel can use to hold memory pages that are not in use, making more room in RAM.

questions.title: Clean /tmp
questions.text: Why do many systems clean `/tmp` at boot?

options.t: Temporary files are not meant to survive a reboot, and leftovers could fill the disk or confuse programs.
Because `/tmp` is stored in the boot loader.
Because the kernel cannot mount it otherwise.
